Supervisor's note, accounts team, by Ramesh
Since the rumours about the office merger began, Sabina has seemed different from the others. At lunch the team talks of nothing else. Sabina listens, then goes back to reconciling invoices, calm and quick. Last week I asked how she manages it. She showed me a small green notebook. "When a worry comes during work, I write one line and close it," she said. "At five-thirty I open it, give myself twenty minutes, and actually think it through." Today I saw her at five-thirty in the empty pantry, notebook open, chewing her pen, looking worried for real. Then she wrote a short list of questions and put the notebook away.
What I did next: I offered her a fixed Friday slot with me to bring the questions she can't answer herself. She brought three this Friday, and I answered two honestly and promised to find out the third.

Thursday, 7 pm, my worry hour
It's the time I've kept for this every Thursday since March. Chai on the balcony, notebook, phone on silent.
This week's box: a parent emailed the principal saying I mark her son unfairly. I read the email at 10 am and felt my stomach drop. Then I had four classes to teach. So I wrote "parent email" on a sticky note, stuck it inside my diary, and taught. I actually taught well. The Class 7 poem lesson went brilliantly.
Now it's seven, and I'm letting myself feel it. I'm hurt. I'm also a little scared the principal believes her. Okay. What can I do? Pull out the boy's last three tests and my marking notes. Ask Ankita, who co-teaches that class, to look at them with me tomorrow. Request a meeting with the parent, not an email war.
Done. Box closed till tomorrow.
Mahima

qa.a: Mahima wrote "parent email" on a sticky note and stuck it inside the diary.

qa.a: Asking Ankita to look over the tests and marking notes, because a colleague's second look is concrete help before meeting the parent.

"You didn't open my message."
"What message?"

"Why?"

"I'm sorry. Can I read it now? With you here?"

"This would've been a five-minute talk on Monday," she said quietly.
"I know."

Dear Lavanya,
Remember my big plan to do yoga every morning for thirty days? I told you on the phone before you moved to Pune. Well, I did eleven days straight. I even made a chart with stickers.

Nirmala

Tuesday. The gas cylinder ran out in the middle of Jeevan's dal. Lalremsiami, his flatmate, sighed loudly. "You never book the cylinder. You always mess these things up." Jeevan's ears went hot. "Never? I booked it in March!" "Once!" They argued for twenty minutes about March and "never" and "always". Nobody booked the cylinder. They ate bread.
Friday. Still no gas. Jeevan kept replaying the words. It felt like being painted as useless, and he didn't want to talk to her at all. She left a note, "Gas???", and he felt defensive just reading it.
The next Sunday. Jeevan took a breath and knocked. "Can we skip never and always? What's the actual problem?" Lalremsiami sat down. "I end up booking it every time, and I'm tired." They stuck a list on the fridge: odd months Jeevan, even months her. The cylinder came on Monday.

qa.a: Jeevan felt painted as useless, hurt and defensive, so he argued about the words rather than the gas.

qa.a: Jeevan asked to skip "never" and "always" and asked what the actual problem was, which led to a simple rota.

qa.a: She was tired of always booking the cylinder, and her frustration came out as "never" and "always".

subtype: Hearing black-and-white judgements [Receiver]
passage: Gargi, you're fighting with your roommate over words? Let your Sonali Mami tell you about Hostel Room 12. I was twenty, in a working women's hostel in Nagpur. My roommate Usha was sharp. One day she said, "You never clean the bathroom. You always leave hair in the drain." Never! Always! I was so hurt I nearly cried. I shouted back, "I cleaned it last Tuesday!" We fought for a week about that Tuesday. Nobody cleaned anything. The drain got worse. Then one night, too tired to fight, I asked her, "Forget never. What do you want to be different?" She paused. "I just want it cleaned on Sundays. By someone. Not always me." So we made a Sunday rota, alternate weeks. We stayed roommates for three years. That day I learnt: when someone says "never", don't fight the word. Ask for the problem underneath.
